course: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer – Professional (AIP-C01)
part_title: Lab 12 — Diagnose and Roll Back GenAI Deployment Regression
review_basis: Actual original slides 68–74 visually inspected, including bundle manifests, canary metrics, isolated A/B tests, compatible index rollback and safety release gates.

scenes.title: Scenario and release dependency graph
scenes.narration: A new application release, B, is producing more errors, greater latency and worse grounded answer quality than release A. The architecture makes it clear that a release is not just one model identifier. Follow the application configuration into Bedrock inference, retrieval embeddings and OpenSearch index, plus CloudWatch telemetry. The release manifest on the right binds model v2, RAG configuration B, prompt version three, embedding model v2 and a compatible index identifier. The sample logs contrast release A with latency eight hundred twenty milliseconds, no errors and groundedness point nine three, against release B with latency two thousand one hundred forty milliseconds, five errors and groundedness point seven one. Those are illustrative fixtures, not real production measurements. Open the application's versioned release manifest and traffic-routing log, and capture the exact bundle serving the failing user cohort. Do not assume Bedrock offers a universal rollback alias for every model. The application controls routing, caching, citations and buffering, so any of those may have changed. Establish the known-good bundle before beginning experiments.

scenes.title: Capture versions and comparable baseline
scenes.narration: The first investigation task is reproducibility. Use an unchanged golden dataset, the same inputs, source files and evaluation order for both release A and release B. The two manifest panels reveal multiple differences: application version, model ID, configuration ID, prompt hash, embedding model and vector index, while some generation settings such as top K and temperature remain equal in the example. Save the complete manifest and each prompt hash, not just a friendly release label. The lower sample baseline shows fifty of fifty test inputs completed for the older release and records its average latency and output hash. Repeat the same test for the candidate under comparable load and capture quality, latency, error, token and cost results. Model identifiers shown on the slide are historical examples, not deployment recommendations. If the embedding model changed but the vector index was not rebuilt compatibly, retrieval may fail independently of model generation. Preserve input snapshots and result provenance so the comparison remains valid after the traffic route changes.

scenes.title: Inspect canary metrics and quality failures
scenes.narration: Now inspect the application's custom canary monitoring rather than looking for a fictional native Bedrock traffic-split screen. The diagram has application-controlled routing to release A and candidate B, with separate quality and performance metrics for each group. The synthetic configuration routes fifty percent of traffic to each for this example; in a real rollout begin with a risk-appropriate smaller percentage and defined halt conditions. The metrics panel shows release A with p95 latency eight hundred fifty milliseconds, groundedness ninety-five percent, errors point five percent and a low per-successful-request cost. Candidate B has p95 two thousand four hundred milliseconds, groundedness seventy-two percent, errors three point one percent, more tokens and higher cost. Inspect a representative golden set including vector search explanations, model pricing and policy summaries; compare cited evidence, not only score averages. Record the actual cohort, release ID, model and index bundle with every trace. The candidate underperforms across several axes, so stop further promotion while isolating causes. Do not compensate for low groundedness by simply increasing output tokens.

scenes.title: Isolate model prompt embedding and config changes
scenes.narration: To diagnose a multi-component release regression, change one variable at a time against a pinned baseline. The top row suggests four experiments: switch only the model or model configuration, switch only the prompt, change only the compatible embedding and index pair, and vary generation settings separately. Use the same golden cohort in every test. The architecture separates retrieval from generation so you can compare their timings without attributing slow search to the foundation model. The sample harness includes model B, a prompt template, embedding model, index name, top K, temperature and maximum tokens. The trace output shows average retrieval about six hundred ninety milliseconds and average generation roughly eighteen hundred twenty-eight in the example. If only retrieval changes, focus on embedding or index compatibility, ingestion and search. If generation alone regresses, inspect model settings, prompt size and response behavior. Never swap to a different embedding dimension against an incompatible index and call the results comparable. Save each experiment's manifest hash and test outcomes.

scenes.title: Roll back routing and compatible index safely
scenes.narration: Once the regression is confirmed, restore a known-good *bundle*, not an isolated model field. The diagram routes production traffic to release A with prompt one, embedding A and compatible index A, while retaining the failing prompt two, embedding B and index B combination for diagnosis. In the application configuration, update model routing, prompt selection and index choice together; also verify application caching, citations and buffering continue to use compatible values. A small controlled canary after rollback should reproduce successful golden questions and acceptable p95 latency. The sample log shows five of five questions passing with citations and about one point eight seconds p95, but this is only a demonstration. Do not delete the candidate index or evidence before understanding the failure. The warning is explicit: Bedrock does not supply one universal model-alias rollback button that changes every model, prompt, application route and vector index. This rollback is implemented through the application's own versioned configuration and supported resources. Keep the previous manifest, routing table and test evidence for audit and a future corrected rollout.

scenes.title: Re-test quality latency cost and safety gates
scenes.narration: A release gate needs measured output evidence, not confidence in a synthetic success banner. The slide's application rule evaluates factual support, citation validity, safety, p95 latency and token or cost budgets using fixed golden cases. The example configuration sets an illustrative p95 limit of two thousand milliseconds, eight hundred maximum tokens and two cents estimated cost, with designated critical cases that block promotion. The sample critical case returns an answer with a citation and passes safety and factual checks, but its measured latency is three thousand one hundred twenty milliseconds, exceeding the stated latency budget. The release must fail despite other metrics passing. In the simulator, evaluate measured responses against the actual thresholds configured for your deployment and ensure every critical failure is visible with its case ID. A single good average cannot compensate for a critical unauthorized, unsupported or over-latency result. Include negative and regression fixtures, not only favorable prompts. Once the known-good bundle passes all gates, maintain alerts on quality, error rate, p95 latency and cost and record the rollback readiness status.

scenes.title: Verify staged promotion and rollback readiness
scenes.narration: Finish with a staged canary plan and an exercised rollback. The slide illustrates successive traffic allocations of five, twenty-five, fifty and one hundred percent, each contingent on quality, safety, latency and cost checks. Those percentages are an example rollout strategy, not a mandatory service feature. The routing and gating belong to your application, with a versioned rollback manifest and a compatible retrieval index preserved for the previous release. The sample events show a candidate deployed at five percent, progressing to twenty-five and fifty after successful gates, then a p95 latency warning. Promotion stops and the application routes back to the prior release using the stored manifest. Verify that the cache, prompt, model selection, embedding/index compatibility and citation policy are restored, not merely the marketing version label. Run the original failing fixture again and confirm latency and groundedness recover without introducing safety regressions. Preserve diagnostic logs, release manifests and required indexes, and only clean obsolete test versions after evidence-retention requirements are met. This completes a defensible release process that can detect, contain and recover from AI deployment regressions.
